 The claimant, XXXXXXXX, is a 24-year-o ld citizen of Israel, who made her refugee claim in Canada on December 9, 1 998. She is an Arab Israeli and Roman Catholic. On XXXXX, 1990, at the age of 14, she was compelled to marry her first cousin XXXXXXXXX in a family-arranged marriage that had her father’s consent. She said that he was pressured by the rest of his family to agree to the marriage. She subsequently moved from her home of Ramallah to Nazareth to live with these cousins she had never seen before. She said that even though the law stated she had to be at least 16 years of age the marriage went ahead. She said a Greek Orthodox priest was bribed and documents were altered to show her to be 17. She said that her signature was forged on the marriage certificate. She said that the Orthodox priest was used because he was willing to perform the ceremony. Meanwhile her mother, two brothers and some other relatives soon left Israel to pursue a succe ssful refugee claim in Canada that centred around a land dispute unrelated to the claimant’s situation.
1 Her father was to remain behind until 1992. After her marriage he came over a few times for dinner and remembers he once had a physical confronta tion with her husband. But she never saw anyone from her immediate family for several y ears after he left the country in February 1992. Meanwhile, the claimant said that her husband and in-laws at their family home constantly abused her. She said her mother-in-law would lock her in the bedroom. She said that she could not run away because she was so poor she could not even buy a postage stamp. She added that her mother-i n-law always hovered around her as well. She said she was never left alone. The claimant and her husband decided to come to Canada as visitors and remained from March 1996 and October 1997. He initia ted an application for them to become permanent residents but the effort was ultimate ly unsuccessful. She said that during this time he became more addicted to gamblin g and started dating strippers. After Immigration asked them to leave they returned to Israel only to return to Canada in 
 
1 The details of the CRDD decision and her mother’s Personal Information Form are in Exhibit C-2.

 2 November 1997. Her husband then again initiated another claim for them to remain as landed immigrants.
2 They had a huge argument two months later and separated on XXXXXX, 1998 as he continued to date exo tic dancers. Meanwhile, she started dating a Canadian landed immigrant, XXXXXXXX , and became pregnant. However, her estranged and enraged husband confronted both her and her new boyfriend. She witnessed a fight at a coffee shop where her hus band threatened her boyfriend. During a tussle, her husband swung a chair at her boyfriend who retaliated by hitting him over the head with a cell phone. She does not know where her former husband is now. He could be in either Canada or Israel. But, she said , she fears his family and is terrified that she could be a victim of a family honour killing if she were to return to Israel. She said she has shamed his family because she has be come pregnant by someone else, her child carries the name of her new companion a nd her ex-husband (they were divorced on XXXXXXX, 1999) is unable to father any ch ildren. The claimant also subsequently remarried on XXXXXX, 1999. She said his family (which is so large that there are 39 first cousins altogether between her and his family) would hunt her down all over Israel and said he has two brothers who travel ev erywhere including Tel Aviv and Haifa. She said her ex-husband has the potential for violence. She said he used to beat up a former fiance and never did that to her only because she never gave him a chance to do so. She said his family was not always violent but remembers males in his family frequently beating up their wives. A paternal uncle, XXXXXXX, testified as a witness. He said he suggested she make a refugee claim.
3 He confirmed the claimant’s story and said her marriage was highly illegal. He said he opposed the marriag e but that his brother, the claimant’s father, approved. He said that her former in-laws knew of her pregnancy and remarriage and he 
 
2 Her ex-husband’s non-attendance at Immigration interviews and his criminal record hampered that effort.

 3 feared for her life if she were to return to Israel. He said the claimant’s father would not testify because of the delicate family situation involving family members in Israel and in particular did not want to take a stand agains t his former son-in-law’s father, who is his brother. The claimant had said that this un cle had originally opposed her first marriage but he was second in authority behind her father. ANALYSIS The panel carefully considered the evidence adduced, all representations, and the relevant statutory provisions and case law. The panel finds the claimant is a member of a particular social group, women. The pane l also considered the Guidelines on Women
 Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution
: Update issued by the Chairperson pursuant to section 65(3) of the Immigration Act
 on November 25, 1996. The panel finds the claimant to be a cr edible witness. The panel finds she was straightforward and genuine in her demeanour. It finds she was forcibly conscripted into an illegal marriage at age 14 and was kept as a virtual hostage of her in-laws. The panel finds her “marriage” amounted to statutory ra pe without her consent. The panel also finds she was mentally abused and physica lly confined by her in-laws and ex-husband during this period. She said she fears returni ng to Israel as an Arab Israeli who would be the victim of an Arab honour killing by her former in-laws or possible retribution from her ex-spouse who may now be in Israel. The panel considered the documentation on this subject matter i.e. honour killings involving Arab women to see if her claim is objectively well founded and whether she could reasonably access protection. Exhibit R-1 at item 2.1
4 states that as of February 26, 1999 violence against all women is a problem in Israel. The Israeli government has allocated minimal funds for a special campaign to combat such violence. Groups that focus on domestic violence 
 
3 The claimant testified her delay in making a refugee claim was due to the conflicting advice of this uncle who suggested she initiate her claim and her father who wanted to have her remain in her first husband’s application for permanent residence. The panel accepted this explanation in light of the family dynamic that had her father supporting the marriage while her uncle opposing it as the uncle’s further testimony reveals. The claimant said she also felt cl oser to her uncle than to her father. 
4 1998 Country Reports on Human Rights Practices, U.S. Department of State

T99-07761 
 4 include a committee established by the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs that includes Jewish and Arab nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) and government

 5 representatives. Their husbands or other male relatives killed thirteen women during 1998. Some 200,000 women suffer from domestic violence each year, and some seven per cent of these are abused on a regular basis. An estimated 60,000 women were sexually assaulted or abused in 1997. Only a small percentage of victims complained to the police. An estimated 60 per cent of victims were 18 or under. Arab human rights advocates also have formed a coalition to ra ise public awareness of honour killings. At least five of the 13 women killed during the year by male relatives were killed in family honour killings. The government supports 10 shelters for battered women, including one exclusively for Christian, Muslim, and Dr uze women and one for both non-Jewish and Jewish women. Women’s right advocates consider this number inadequate. The U.S. State Department updated this material in their report dated February 25, 2000.
5 It stated that violence against women continued to be a problem. There continued to be government action to reduce violen ce against women in Jewish and Arab communities. However, the government cont inued to allocate minimal funds for a special campaign to combat such violence. In 1999, their husband or other male relatives killed 17 women. Three of the victims were killed in family honour cases in the Arab community. In light of this contradictory material the panel asked the RCO to commission a new Response to Information Request thro ugh the Research Directorate of the Immigration and Refugee Board.
6 The query sought to update the circumstances of the honour killings mentioned in the U.S. State Department reports including the profiles of the perpetrators and the reaction by Israeli authorities. The June 9, 2000 response reported th e honour killing of a young Arab woman who had complained to the police that she was being abused by her father who eventually was arrested and was sentenced to 14 months in jail. 
 
5 Exhibit R-3

 6 The response quoted the Women’s Internati onal Network as stating that in Israel many Muslim women are killed to preserve family honour.
7 It cites a dramatic rise in killings carried out by male relatives among Muslims in Israel, the West Bank and Gaza after alleged sexual misconduct. “There ar e no reliable statistics on the number of Palestinian or Bedouin women killed each year for transgressing the strict moral code that governs traditional family life … The women may be killed because they go out alone, are seen talking to a man or becaus e of rumours they are sleeping with a man outside marriage.”
8 In its July 1997 report to the Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW) Israel formally co mmented on the issue of honour killings. Firstly, Israel has stated that it abhors practices such as honour killings and stated that its Supreme Court has condemned the practice a nd handed down a sentence of 18 years in one case. “The increased awareness of la w enforcement authorities has been expressed through unobtrusive activities directed at moving the girl or woman in danger beyond the reach of family members.”
9 The Israeli representative also stated that “the police force had focused special attention to the unique ness of the Arab population and to Arab women’s higher risk of falling victim to domes tic violence, in all its courses, training sessions and contacts with field units.”
10 Currently, four Arab women serve on the police force and the police operated in the Arab communities with the same procedures which governed its operation in Jewish communities, according to which a woman victim of sexual assault has to be questioned by a female investigator. One of the 12 shelters for battered women was in an Arab village and fully financed by the government. “In addition, there were two halfway houses which accommodated Arab women and girls following their stay in shelters. Plus, out of the 100 posts for social workers who treated

 7 girls in distress, 20 were held by Arab social workers. There were 11 hotlines in Israel, two of which served Arab communities. According to police data, in 1996 there were 13,600 complaints of spousal abuse brough t by Jewish women and 1,367 complaints brought by Arab women. As far as sexual o ffenses were concerned, there were 1,972 brought by Jewish women as opposed to 117 brought by Arab women…”
11 In a June 1997 report, the Contempor ary Women’s Issues publication indicated that from 1990 until 1997 there were 52 honour killings involving Palestinian women and girls. “This number does not reflect the full extent of the problem, as many women are missing and their fate is unknown.”
12 Furthermore, “Judicial proceedings ar e often influenced by the fact that Palestinian society condones honour killing fo r purposes of protecting family honour. Most judges and the police still regard these acts as the private concern of the family and as a phenomenon that stems from the social nor ms and values of traditional Palestinian society, thus concluding that their judgement s must be culturally sensitive. For this reason, many judges accept the argument that th e murderer lost control of himself as a victim of the same values and norms which perpetrate honour killing. This is also apparent in the manner in which the state pros ecutor charges the accused. Rather than pursuing a charge of pre-meditated murder, th e accused is charged with the lesser crime of manslaughter. “Likewise, the Israeli police often mish andle cases of Palestinian females whose lives are endangered by their families. Women who file complaints with the police are not taken seriously, and their problems are often ignored. Frequently, they are returned home because of the widely accepted belief th at the place of a Palestinian woman is in her home.
13 The panel has considered the totality of the documentary evidence including the fact that honour killings among Arab women have claimed at least 60 victims in the

 8 1990s,
14 and the efforts of the Israeli government to combat these crimes and at times its undeniably inadequate response. The pane l concludes the claimant faces a serious possibility of being persecuted should she return to Israel. The panel has considered her credible testimony including the fact that she faces a crazed ex-family that believes she has shamed her family by her divorce, remarriage and giving birth to a child bitterly contrasting the fact that her ex-husband ca nnot father a child. The panel has also considered her particular circumstances and th e specific evidence before it in concluding that in her case she could not access adequate state protection. The panel finds that given its track record the Israeli State would be willing to protect her but concludes on a balance of probabilities that she would not receive adequate protection. The panel could not ignore the frequency of honour killings among Arab women, the mixed record in dealing with them and the unique relationshi p and context of Arab cultural mores and practices within the Israeli state and the difficulty this poses in accessing protection.
15 The panel also notes the test for assessing risk is more than a mere possibility of persecution which the panel finds exists in this case especially given the violent history of the claimant’s in-laws including the arrangeme nt of an illegal marriage and her virtual kidnapping and imprisonment. The panel also noted the ex-husband’s propensity for violence directed at women and his physical confrontation with the claimant’s husband and father.
